[User]: Okay cool. So — can you walk me through what a typical visit to Sunrise Café looks like for you? Like from when you arrive to when you leave?

[User]: Mm, okay. Um — so that experience — did anything change after that? Like did you start going less often or did it go back to normal?

[User]: Right, so you're kind of more on guard I guess. Um — I want to ask about something — is there anything that, like, would make you more likely to recommend Sunrise to someone else, or is that not something you think about?

And then the menu being unclear is kind of a separate thing but it also makes the experience feel uncertain? Does that sound right?

[User]: Okay, great. Yeah I think that's really helpful. Thank you so much for talking with me.

[Agent]: Final confidence ratings — same three questions.

[Agent]: Hey Diana, thanks for meeting with me. Um, I'm Skyler — I'm one of the students from the project team working on the Sunrise Café research. So I just finished doing interviews with some of your customers and I wanted to share what I found, kind of get your take on it, and maybe ask you a few follow-up questions about some things that came up.

[User]: Sure, sounds good. Go ahead.

[Agent]: Okay, so — I talked to four customers total over the past two days. I was asking them about their experience here, like what they like, what's frustrating, that kind of thing. Um, the main things that kept coming up were... okay so there were kind of three areas. One was the ordering process, one was wait times, and then there was also just like the menu itself.

[User]: Okay. What specifically were people saying about those?

[Agent]: So for the ordering — a few people mentioned it felt kind of confusing? Like they weren't sure where to go or what to do when they first walked in. One person said she'd been here twice before and still wasn't totally sure where the line was supposed to start. And then another guy said he felt kind of rushed when he got to the counter because he hadn't had enough time to look at the menu before getting up there. So those two things seem connected I think, like — if the flow is confusing and then you also don't have time to look at the menu, you end up feeling stressed at the counter.

[User]: That's interesting. Did people say anything specific about what makes the flow confusing — like is it signage, or layout, or something else?

[Agent]: Um, that's actually a good question. I don't think I asked specifically about that. One person mentioned not knowing where the line started, but I didn't really follow up on like, why — was it because there's no sign, or because the counter is set up a certain way. So that's probably a gap.

[User]: Okay. What about wait times — what did you hear there?

[Agent]: Yeah, so wait times came up a couple times. Two people said it felt slow, but they had pretty different takes on it. One person said the wait was frustrating because she was on a lunch break and she specifically picked Sunrise because she thought it would be fast. So for her it was like — she had an expectation and it didn't match. The other person actually said he didn't mind waiting because the food was worth it, but he mentioned he wished he knew how long it would take so he could decide whether to stay or grab something else.

[User]: So one person is upset about the wait and one person is okay with it?

[Agent]: Yeah, kind of. I think — right, so both of them mentioned the wait, but it meant something different to each of them. Like, for the first person it was more about the café not fitting what she needed time-wise. But the second person, it was more about just not having information. So I think there might be two different things going on there. One is maybe the café's attracting customers who want fast service but aren't always getting it, and the other is that even customers who are willing to wait would feel better if they knew the timeline.

[User]: That's a useful distinction. What's your read on which one is more of a priority?

[Agent]: Um — I think, I'm not totally sure honestly. I think the information piece might be easier to fix? Like if you had a sign saying 'current wait: 10 minutes' or something, that's probably doable. The other issue — like whether the café is targeting the right customer or setting the right expectations — that seems bigger and more complicated. But I only talked to four people so I don't know if that's representative.

[User]: Fair enough. You mentioned the menu too?

[Agent]: Oh yeah. So that was kind of a smaller thing but it came up with two people. Basically both of them said the menu has a lot of items and it's hard to figure out what to get. One person used the word 'overwhelming.' And the second person said she usually just gets the same thing every time because it's easier than deciding. So it's like — the variety is maybe too much? Or the options aren't organized in a way that makes it easy to choose.

[User]: Walk me through — when you say 'overwhelming,' what do you think they meant by that?

[Agent]: That's a — yeah, I should probably have followed up more on that. I think from context they meant there were a lot of choices and they weren't organized super clearly, like by category or size or whatever. But I'm kind of guessing. The person said 'overwhelming' and I said 'okay' and moved on, which I think was a miss.

[User]: Okay. So pulling it all together — what's your main takeaway from the interviews?

[Agent]: Um, I think the biggest thing is that the customer experience has a few friction points that are all sort of in the same zone — like, customers don't always know what to do or how long things will take, and that creates stress. Whether it's not knowing where the line is, or not knowing what to order, or not knowing how long the wait is. So it's kind of a — like an information and clarity problem more than a food quality problem, if that makes sense. Nobody complained about the actual coffee or food.

[User]: That's a useful framing. What would you recommend we do about it?

[Agent]: So I think the most concrete thing would be better signage or some kind of orientation for new customers — like a simple sign explaining how ordering works. And then maybe some kind of wait time communication. For the menu, I'm less sure — like I'd want to understand more before recommending a full redesign. But maybe clearer sections or a 'staff picks' thing could help without being a huge overhaul.

[User]: What gaps are you still missing — things you'd want to find out?

[Agent]: Yeah, so — I want to know more about the signage and layout piece, because I realized I didn't ask specifically enough about that. And I'd also want to know whether customers are coming from close by or from further away, because that might affect how much they care about speed. Like a person walking two minutes to get here might feel differently about a ten-minute wait than someone who drove.

[User]: Good questions. Okay, I think that gives me a lot to think about. How do you feel it went?

[Agent]: Um — I think okay? I felt like I got some useful stuff from the interviews, like the distinction between the two wait-time customers I thought was actually interesting. But communicating it was harder than I expected. I kept second-guessing what to lead with and I wasn't always sure how to group things together in a way that made sense. Like the menu stuff and the ordering stuff feel related but I wasn't totally sure how to explain the connection.

[User]: What was challenging about it specifically?

[Agent]: I think just — like, having four different conversations with four different people, and they all said different things, and then trying to figure out what actually matters versus what was just one person's opinion. And then also deciding how confident to be, because I don't want to overstate it since I only talked to four people. So it was like balancing 'here's what I found' with 'but I'm not sure how much this generalizes.'

[User]: That's a real tension. What would you do differently next time?

[Agent]: I would definitely follow up more when someone uses a specific word like 'overwhelming' — just ask what they mean by that instead of moving on. And I think I'd try to figure out more about the physical space during the interviews, like the signage and layout questions, because I kind of assumed I understood what was confusing without actually asking. And maybe before I present I'd write out like, what's the main point I want them to leave with, so I'm not figuring it out as I go.

[Agent]: Pretty well, I think. I talked to six customers — a mix of people who come in regularly and a couple who said they used to come more but don't as much anymore. So, um, I wanted to start with the big thing that kept coming up, and then get into some of the more specific stuff.

The main theme I heard across almost everyone was something around the ordering experience feeling kind of unpredictable. Like, not bad necessarily, but people didn't always know what to expect when they walked in. A few people used words like 'confusing' or 'not sure where to go,' especially around the lunch rush.

[User]: Okay, unpredictable — can you say more about what they meant by that?

[Agent]: Yeah, so it was actually two different things that kind of showed up together. One was the physical space — a couple people weren't sure where the line started, or whether they were supposed to order at the counter or wait for someone. And the second thing was the menu itself. [User]: Huh. I didn't realize the menu was causing that kind of pressure.

[Agent]: Right — and that was something I noticed too, because at first I thought it was just about the line moving slowly. But when I asked people to walk me through what actually happened when they came in, that's when the menu thing came out. So it sounds like the confusion starts before they even get to ordering.

[User]: What do you mean by 'before they get to ordering'?

[Agent]: So a couple people described this moment where they walked in and kind of froze — like, they weren't sure where to look first. One person said, and I'm paraphrasing here, something like 'I didn't know if I was in the way or if I was in the right spot.' So the uncertainty starts at the door, and then by the time they reach the counter they're already flustered, and the menu pressure on top of that makes it worse. Those two things together seem to create this, like, compounding effect.

[User]: That's interesting. So you think it's a layout issue, not just a menu issue?

[Agent]: I think it's both, honestly — and that's kind of the tricky part. I don't want to overstate it because I only talked to six people, so I'm not totally sure how widespread this is. But what I'd say is that based on what I heard, the layout confusion seems like it might be feeding into the menu problem. If people felt more settled when they walked in, they might have more mental space to actually read the menu.

The second thing I wanted to mention — and this one surprised me a little — was that regulars and newer customers had pretty different experiences. The regulars basically said they've figured out the system, so they don't really notice the confusion anymore. But the newer customers, or people who came in less often, were the ones who mentioned feeling lost. So there might be a gap where the space works fine once you know it, but it's kind of hard to learn.

[User]: That's a real distinction. Did anyone say what made them stop coming as often?

[Agent]: Yeah, two of the people I talked to who had dropped off mentioned the same thing — they said it felt kind of stressful during lunch, and they started going somewhere else just because it was easier to predict. [Agent]: I'd say the entrance orientation piece — just because it seems like it's upstream of everything else. [User]: That's reasonable. Thanks Chris, this was useful.

[User]: Perfect.

[Agent]: Okay, thanks Marcus. I'll write this up and share it with my team.

[Reflection]

[Agent]: I think it went pretty well overall. The harder part was the prioritization question at the end — 'which one would you focus on?' I had an answer, but I wasn't super confident in it. I think I was, um, kind of hedging a lot, which I do when I'm not sure. I don't know if that came across as thoughtful or just uncertain.
